rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may collect a security deposit of at most 1.5 times one month's rent, including any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security. Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account, and the interest belongs to the tenant. The landlord must give the tenant written notice of the bank, the amount and the interest rate within 30 days of receipt. The deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions, must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Return is due within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x one month's rent (no more than 2.5x rent at lease inception including first month's rent); annual increase max 10% of current deposit; return within 30 days of termination with itemized deductions; 5 business days if displaced by fire/flood/condemnation; double damages plus fees for wrongful withholding; 7% per annum applied to rent if notice or interest is not provided

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Interest-bearing account rules differ for landlords holding deposits for ten or fewer units versus ten or more units
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rentals, including mobile homes. Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant requests compliance in writing.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling exempt; the tenant may make the law apply 30 days after a written request to the landlord
coverage.other_conditions: The interest-bearing account provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals of 125 consecutive days or less

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (unless the tenant requests coverage in writing); seasonal rentals are exempt from the interest-account provisions
rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant
rules.review_note: The guide also describes deposit return within 15 business days when a tenant ends a lease under the Safe Housing Act (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19). This is folded into the main record.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statutes).

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not evict a tenant or fail to renew a lease without good cause. The statutory causes include nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct, property damage, breach of rules or lease covenants, an unpaid and non-unconscionable rent increase, health and safety removal, permanent retirement from residential use, refusal of reasonable lease changes, habitual late payment, condominium or cooperative conversion, owner or buyer occupancy, end of employment-based tenancy, and certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses. A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment, and a Notice to Cease is required for some causes. Notice periods vary by cause. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can lawfully remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance. Landlords who misuse the unit after eviction face treble damages.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit before filing suit: 3 days (disorderly conduct, damage, employment end, drug/assault/theft offenses); 1 month (rule/lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion owner/buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety removal); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation assistance for illegal occupancy: 6x monthly rent. Treble damages plus fees for post-eviction misuse; civil penalty up to $10,000 for residential reuse within 5 years of a retirement or demolition eviction

unverifiable_exemptions: Unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it
Hotel, motel or guest house rented to a transient or seasonal guest
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rentals, including single-family homes, mobile homes and parks, apartment buildings and rooming and boarding houses. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are subject only to a narrower list of causes.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings may be evicted only for listed causes: holdover after lease expiry, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, willful damage, repeated rule violations, and lease violations where re-entry is reserved. Notice to quit is 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancies, 1 month for month-to-month, and 3 days for disorderly, destructive or rule-violation causes.
coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel guests with no alternate residence who live there continuously are covered. Landlords who have not properly registered cannot evict.

rules.exemptions: Hotel, motel and guest house transient or seasonal guests; units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member; owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are covered only by a narrower list of causes
rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord must have good cause to evict a tenant (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53).
rules.review_note: The guide's exceptions paragraph for owner-occupied premises is worded ambiguously ("two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two (2) or fewer rental units"). The later section on owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings is used for the coverage description. Relocation assistance, penalties and the unconscionable-increase standard are folded into this record.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statutes).

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer who wants to occupy a foreclosed property as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit, and a tenant with a longer lease may not be evicted until the lease expires. A person who acquires a foreclosed property with rental units must give tenants a notice in English and Spanish within 10 business days of the sale, stating that ownership has changed and tenants need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. Any monetary offer to induce tenants to leave must come with a separate notice and a five-day review period, and pressure tactics are barred.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit; tenant-rights notice within 10 business days after sale (English and Spanish); 5-day review period for buyout offers

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice requirement. Posting replaces individual notices in buildings with more than 10 units.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only when a foreclosed property is sold or transferred

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey.
rules.review_note: The guide does not cite a specific statute for the 90-day notice to quit. The citation reflects the Foreclosure Fairness Act sections it names for the notice duties.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statutes).

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of the lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when the tenant exercises certain civil rights. These include enforcing rights under the lease or law, making a good-faith complaint to a governmental authority after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing time to correct the problem, organizing or joining a lawful tenant organization, and refusing lease changes made in retaliation. A tenant may sue for damages.

coverage.summary: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings exempt

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10).
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statute).

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (condominium/cooperative conversion)
rules.requirement: Qualifying senior, permanently disabled, or disabled-veteran tenants in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership may keep a protected tenancy and be protected from eviction for up to 40 years. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date, and their income must be within the stated limit. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of their right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 extends similar protections to qualified Hudson County tenants.
rules.key_value: Protected from eviction for 40 years; income not more than 3x the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; applications generally within 60 days

unverifiable_exemptions: Tenant eligibility: age 62 or older before the recording date, permanent disability, or disabled veteran status
coverage.summary: Applies to eligible tenants in buildings being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 applies only in Hudson County, the only qualified county.
coverage.other_conditions: Tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
citation_aliases: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act
rules.quoted_span: The Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act protects senior citizens who meet certain eligibility requirements (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22 to -61.39; N.J.A.C. 5:24-2.1 to -2.11).
rules.review_note: The Hudson County Tenant Protection Act of 1992 is folded into this record rather than given its own record.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statutes).

rules.title: Rent increase limit after condominium/cooperative conversion
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Rents may still be increased to cover the cost of new services or amenities. The prohibition applies to all tenants in the building, whether or not they qualify for protected tenancy as seniors or disabled persons.

coverage.summary: Applies to tenants in buildings converted or being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).
rules.review_note: The quoted span reproduces a spacing typo in the source ("cos ts"). The state has no general rent cap; the Anti-Eviction Act also requires that rent increases not be unconscionable.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statute).

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental
rules.requirement: The Law Against Discrimination bars discrimination in renting housing. This includes refusing to rent on the basis of source of lawful income, familial status, disability and other listed characteristics. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, an oversized family, a zoning-violating occupancy, or poor credit history. Landlords may charge for credit reports, ask for reasonable application fees, and run public-records background checks.
rules.key_value: Fines up to $10,000 for a first offense

unverifiable_exemptions: Rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home
Residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex, and age-restricted housing (as to familial status)
coverage.summary: Applies to all landlord-tenant relationships except two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and certain single-sex or age-restricted residences.

rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex and age-restricted housing as to familial status
rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.
rules.review_note: The guide is a general summary. The listed fines and the owner-occupied exemptions come from other passages of the same section.
rules.source_notes: Official state DCA guide (secondary summary of the statute).

no_rule_findings.finding: The state has no rent control or general limit on rent increases. Municipalities may adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years, and some subsidized rents may also be exempt.
no_rule_findings.quoted_span: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents.

no_rule_findings.finding: The guide says landlords may charge the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees. It states no dollar cap, receipt requirement or refund rule.
no_rule_findings.quoted_span: The landlord may also request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

result.doc_summary: The NJ Department of Community Affairs "Truth in Renting" guide summarizes New Jersey landlord-tenant law. Rules captured here: the Security Deposit Law (1.5x rent cap, 30-day return, double damages), the Anti-Eviction Act (good cause, notice periods, relocation), foreclosure tenant notices, reprisal protections, senior and disabled protected tenancy on conversion, the post-conversion rent increase bar, and the Law Against Discrimination's source-of-income protection. The state has no rent control, though municipalities may adopt it. The guide states no application-fee cap and has no algorithmic rent-setting content.
